The Applicant does not plan to use helicopters for the placement of transmission towers. It is anticipated that the activity involved with the construction of transmission line rights-of-way and facilities would be extensive. It would also be visible to boaters on Lake Jocassee and motorists along South Carolina Route 171, but this impact would be minimal because of the distances involved.
3.1.2 Species and Ecosystems
3.1.2.1 Flora
Approximately 505 acres of vegetation would be cleared from areas designated for various project works such as roads, site laydown areas, the transmission line tower bases, and the upper reservoir area. About 465 acres would be permanently removed from productivity (primarily in the upper reservoir area). The majority of the permanently lost vegetation is second growth forest comprising the plant communities discussed in Subsection 2.2.1. The pine-oak plant community is found generally above elevation 2,800 feet and thus should not be affected. Upon removal of all temporary construction facilities, the vegetation would become reestablished, and if the larger trees are spared, the areas would eventually return to their approximate original conditions within about a year.
As proposed, clearing of the transmission line rights-of-way in mountainous areas would be accomplished by selective clearing to the extent possible. Transmission towers would be placed on the highest elevations when possible. Applicant intends to clear vegetation in areas where line clearances of 30 feet above tree tops is not possible.
3.1.2.2 Terrestrial Fauna
The Bad Creek reservoir site is the largest land unit subject to change within the proposed project boundaries. It currently represents a region of habitat diversity encompassing the dendritic drainage systems of Bad and West Bad Creeks.
Construction of the proposed reservoir, including the dam sites, would eliminate approximately 370 acres of mixed deciduous and coniferous forest. Approximately 2.3 stream miles and associated riparian habitats would be inundated within the Bad Creek and West Bad Creek drainages.
